# (PART) Sampling {-}

# Sampling Distributions {#sampling-distributions}

<div class="draft">Work in progress.</div>

## One Population, Many Samples

- one population, many samples: each sample mean is different
- first: imagine a large population of scores (mean 50, SD 10)

```{r population-scores}
population_scores <- rnorm(n = 10000, mean = 50, sd = 10)

population_summary <- tibble(score = population_scores) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_score = mean(score),
    sd_score = sd(score)
  )

population_summary
```

- population has lots of individual values; draw one sample of 20, get one sample mean

```{r one-sample-mean}
one_sample <- sample(population_scores, size = 20)
mean(one_sample)
```

- try: rerun chunk; different mean each time (different people in each sample)

## Watch The Sampling Process

- collect the means: the sampling distribution
- widget builds distribution of sample means one sample at a time; same population (mean 50, SD 10)
- each time you add a sample, it:

1. draws a sample of people from the population (blue dots, top panel)
2. calculates the mean of that sample (orange line)
3. drops that mean into the bottom panel, which keeps every sample mean so far

<iframe src="apps/sampling/embed.html" width="100%" height="720" title="Sampling distribution interactive widget" style="border: 0;"></iframe>

- try this sequence:

1. **+1** a few times; watch where each sample mean lands: most near 50, but not exactly on it
2. **+10** a few times, then **+100**; shape builds in bottom panel: lots of means close to 50, fewer the further from it
3. compare bottom panel with population in top panel (same x-axis): sample means much less spread out than individual values
4. **SD of the means** = SE estimated by simulation; compare with **Formula SE** (population SD / $\sqrt{n}$, next chapter); closer the more samples you add
5. **Reset**, sample size 5, a few hundred samples; then 50; predict wider or narrower before each run
6. tick **Expected shape** to see the distribution the formula predicts

### Test Your Predictions

- predict first, then check with **Reset** and a few hundred samples each time:

1. sample size from 5 to 50: wider or narrower bottom panel? by about how much?
2. keep adding samples (+100 several times) at the same sample size: does the spread of the means keep shrinking?
3. population SD doubled, sample size unchanged: what happens to the spread of the means?
4. how does the spread of the sample means compare with the spread of the population in the top panel, for any n above 1?

`r hide("Show explanations")`
- n 5 to 50: narrower; SE = SD / $\sqrt{n}$, 10 times the n gives about $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ times narrower
- more samples: no; more samples sharpen the *picture* of the distribution, its spread stays near the SE; only n (and the population SD) change it
- SD doubled: spread of the means doubles too (SE is proportional to SD)
- always narrower than the population: averaging cancels out some of the high and low values
`r unhide()`

## Many Samples In Code

- link to code: **+1** = `one_sample_mean(n = 20)` below (one sample, one mean); **+100** = `map_dbl(1:100, \(i) one_sample_mean(n = 20))`; **SD of the means** = `sd()` of all means collected so far
- repeat that process many times in code to get many sample means:

```{r sample-mean-function}
one_sample_mean <- function(n) {
  one_sample <- sample(population_scores, size = n)
  mean(one_sample)
}

sample_means_20 <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_sample_mean(n = 20))
```

- plot the distribution of sample means

```{r sample-means-visual, fig.cap="A sampling distribution of sample means.", echo=FALSE}
sample_mean_data <- tibble(mean_score = sample_means_20)

ggplot(sample_mean_data, aes(x = mean_score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, colour = "white", fill = "#467AAC") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = mean(sample_means_20),
    linewidth = 1.2,
    colour = "#D55E00"
  ) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r sample-means-visual-code, ref.label="sample-means-visual", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- point out: x-axis is now sample means, not scores; its spread is what the next chapter calls the SE

## Sample Size And Spread

- bigger samples, narrower spread

```{r sample-size-comparison}
sample_means_10 <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_sample_mean(n = 10))
sample_means_50 <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_sample_mean(n = 50))

sample_size_data <- tibble(
  mean_score = c(sample_means_10, sample_means_50),
  sample_size = c(
    rep("n = 10", length(sample_means_10)),
    rep("n = 50", length(sample_means_50))
  )
)
```

```{r sample-size-visual, fig.cap="Larger samples give a narrower distribution of sample means.", echo=FALSE}
ggplot(sample_size_data, aes(x = mean_score, fill = sample_size)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .35) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("n = 10" = "#467AAC", "n = 50" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean", y = "Density", fill = "Sample size") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r sample-size-visual-code, ref.label="sample-size-visual", eval=FALSE, webex.hide="Show the plot code"}
```

- point out: `n = 50` distribution narrower, because larger samples give more stable means
- that is why `n` sits in the denominator of the SE formula (next chapter):

```text
SE = SD / sqrt(n)
```
